intuition: Scan all positions in O(n) time. Binary search exploits the one-drop structure for O(log n). Ordinary binary search cannot compare target with mid alone because a rotation disrupts global ordering, even though most local ordering survives.

At most one rotation drop appears inside the candidate interval. If nums[left] is no larger than nums[mid], the left half has no drop and is sorted. A target between those endpoint values belongs there; all other targets must be sought in the right half. When the left half is not sorted, the right half is. Distinct values remove ambiguous equal-boundary cases and guarantee a substantial reduction on every iteration.

The target, if present, remains inside the candidate interval. A sorted half either contains the target in its numeric range or cannot contain it, so discarding the appropriate half preserves the invariant. The interval shrinks each iteration; exhaustion proves absence. Each iteration discards at least half the candidate positions.

steps: For [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], left=0, right=6, and mid=3 stores 7.
The left half [4,5,6,7] is sorted, but target 0 is outside its value interval.
The left half [0,1] is sorted and contains target 0, so right becomes 4.
Now mid=4 equals the target; return index 4.

codeNotes.note: This endpoint comparison identifies a half with reliable increasing order after the failed equality check.
The half-open value comparison excludes mid because its value was already checked and rejected.
Exhausting the candidate range proves the target is absent rather than merely hidden near the pivot.
